we have shown how to evolve a scalable multi-robot controller using a neural-tissue architecture that permits the emergence of novel behavior through task decomposition.

we have developed an artificial neural tissue (ANT) architecture that can be used for controlling multirobot teams and that this architecture can evolve a scalable controller for a resource-collection task.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and development of a scalable and flexible multirobot controller using a novel neural-tissue paradigm.
the development of a control architecture that is capable of scaling up to larger numbers of robots and to more complex tasks.
the evolution of multirobot controllers using an artificial neural tissue paradigm and the emergence of novel capabilities such as task decomposition.

the ANT paradigm is capable of producing a wide variety of complex behaviors in a multirobot system, and is a viable alternative to traditional approaches.
the artificial neural tissue paradigm has proven itself to be a robust and scalable architecture for multirobot control.
the ANT architecture is a promising approach for developing scalable controllers for autonomous multirobot systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the ANT architecture, which combines a coarse-coding approach with a Darwinian evolutionary process, can evolve a controller for a multirobot task in simulation.
we are able to show the emergence of task decomposition and the ability to solve a complex multirobot task in simulation using a single global fitness criterion.
we have shown that a neural network can be used as an artificial brain for a multi robot team.

a simple neural tissue can be used as the basis for a scalable multirobot controller that exhibits self-organization, task decomposition and the emergence of novel behaviors.
ANT controllers are scalable, robust and can be applied to multirobot tasks.
